message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of any needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act within a reasonable time, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (usually not more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Keep receipts or bank records of payments.
• If you’re late, communicate with the landlord and negotiate a payment plan if needed. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The lease ends automatically unless renewed.
• **Early termination**: Some leases allow early termination for a fee; otherwise, you may be liable for rent until the lease expires. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry to the landlord in writing. | | **Landlord Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries and verify that the notice was given. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may **deduct the cost** from your rent (up to the amount of the repair) and pay the landlord the difference. | • Document the issue, send a written notice, keep receipts, and pay the landlord the remaining rent. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly, attend court hearings, and keep copies of all documents. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent control** laws. | • Be aware that rent increases are typically governed by the lease terms or local ordinances. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease and keep records of payments. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide insurance for your personal property. | • Consider renter’s insurance for protection against theft, fire, or water damage. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for breach of contract, damages, or unlawful eviction. | • Consult an attorney or a tenant advocacy group for guidance. | --- #### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Understand every clause, especially those about rent, deposits, repairs, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of emails, texts, and written notices. Take photos of any maintenance issues. 3. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, use email or certified mail so you have a record. 4. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific time frames for notice, repairs, and deposit returns. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you encounter a problem, contact the TDHCA, TCHR, or a local tenant rights organization before it escalates. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Tenant‑landlord dispute resolution, housing counseling | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Complaint filing for discrimination | https://www.tchr.texas.gov | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Federal fair housing resources | https://www.hud.gov | | **Local Tenant Advocacy Groups** | Legal aid, mediation, education | Search online for “tenant rights Texas” + your city | --- If you have a specific situation (e.g., a dispute over a security deposit, a repair that hasn’t been addressed, or a notice of eviction), let me know and I can give more tailored advice or help you draft a letter to your landlord.
